name: Iceland
summary: A volcanic island settled by Norse people around 874, ruled by Norway and Denmark, sovereign from 1918 and a republic since 1944.

knownFor.label: Althing
knownFor.note: One of the oldest parliaments, founded in 930.

knownFor.label: Geothermal power
knownFor.note: Heat and electricity from volcanic ground.

location.value: A Nordic island country between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean; about 103,000 km².

terrain.value: A volcanic plateau with sand and lava fields, mountains and glaciers.

climate.value: Temperate, warmed by the Gulf Stream, despite lying just south of the Arctic Circle.

resources.value: Fish, and abundant geothermal and hydroelectric power that gives cheap hot water, heating and electricity.

disasters.value: The Laki eruption of 1783–1784 caused a famine that killed nearly a quarter of the population.

population.value: About 395,000 people, the smallest population of any NATO member.

urbanisation.value: More than 70% of people live in the south-west corner (Greater Reykjavík and the nearby Southern Peninsula).

disease.value: Average life expectancy of 81.8 years and a universal health care system.

migration.value: 13.5% of residents (33,678 people) were foreign-born in December 2007; Poles are the largest minority.

economicBase.value: Tourism, fish and fish products, aluminium and ferrosilicon.

tradeRoutes.value: Fishing provides roughly half of all exports; Keflavík International Airport is the main hub for international passengers.

wealth.value: One of the world's wealthiest and most developed nations, with a Nordic welfare system.

inequality.value: One of the lowest levels of income inequality in the world; equality between the sexes is very high.

governmentType.value: A representative democracy and parliamentary republic; the Althing is one of the world's oldest legislative assemblies.

keyRulers.value: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, the world’s first elected woman president (1980).

succession.value: Coalition governments formed after elections, such as the Independence Party with the Progressive Party after 2013.

institutions.value: The Althing, set up by 930 and suspended from 1799 to 1845.

stability.value: Ranked the most peaceful country in the world in the 2024 Global Peace Index.

eliteConflict.value: Party competition, with the centre-right Independence Party often leading coalition governments.

armyAndTech.value: No standing army, only the Icelandic Coast Guard; a US military command, the Iceland Defense Force, was based there from 1951 to 2006.

majorWars.value: The Cod Wars with the United Kingdom over fishing limits (1952–1976), with confrontations between the Icelandic Coast Guard and the Royal Navy.

territoryChange.value: Fishing limits extended to 200 nautical miles, leading to the 1975–1976 Cod War.

alliancesRivals.value: Joined NATO on 30 March 1949; a member of the European Economic Area but not the EU.

inventions.value: The world's largest electricity producer per person, using hydroelectric and geothermal power.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Iceland in Reykjavík is the largest university; deCODE genetics funded a genealogy database of all known Icelanders.

openness.value: Open to trade and tourism (joined the European Economic Area in 1994; 1.7 million visitors in 2016); protective of its fishing grounds (fishing limits extended from 1952 to 1976).

communicationTransport.value: Route 1, the Ring Road (completed in 1974), runs around the island; no passenger railways have ever operated.

religion.value: The Church of Iceland, a Lutheran body, is the state church; Christianity was adopted around 999–1000.

languageWriting.value: Icelandic, which has changed less from Old Norse than other Nordic languages; most people use patronymic surnames (e.g. Jónsdóttir, “Jón's daughter”).

artsArchitecture.value: The medieval sagas, and modern music acts such as Björk and Sigur Rós.

sharedIdentity.value: Icelandic, a North Germanic language from Old Norse, is the only living language to keep the runic letter Þ in Latin script.

dailyLife.value: Cheap geothermal hot water and heating; food based on fish, lamb and dairy, including skyr.

neighbours.value: Closest to Greenland; the nearest European land is the Faroe Islands, then Shetland and Scotland.

ideasReligions.value: Settled by Norwegians from 874; in 1980 Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the world's first democratically elected female head of state.

colonisation.value: Came under Norwegian rule in the 13th century and later Danish rule; a sovereign state in union with Denmark from 1918 and a republic from 1944.

riseSignals.value: Sovereign kingdom in union with Denmark (1918); republic (1944).

peakPeriod.value: After the 2008 crash the economy stabilised and tourism surged.

declineSignals.value: Its three largest banks, Glitnir, Landsbanki and Kaupthing, collapsed in the 2008 financial crisis.
